reasoning: Taa marbuta after ي is e, giving wilaaye. This is the normal word for a US-style state, as in il-wilaayaat il-muttaHide.
ص is emphatic (S) and ق is a glottal stop in this everyday word. Saqr is primarily a falcon, so 'hawk' is only approximate.
مرة in construct state is mart (wife of), so mart khaal is the maternal uncle's wife. Spoken forms like mart il-khaal or mart khaali also occur.
Palestinian 3urs, plural a3raas. The vowel is u, not i. faraH is also used for a wedding celebration.
Taa marbuta after و is e, giving rakwe. It is the small long-handled pot used for Arabic coffee.
A standard word, often seen on packaging, with ق as a glottal stop in speech. For washing powder in conversation, boodra (or boodrit ghasiil) is more typical.
ق is a glottal stop, giving la7a'. It is the everyday verb for catching up with someone or making it in time.
The reply to masa l-khayr. Palestinians drop the hamza (masa) and the article's i after the vowel, so n-nuur. Spoken slowly it can be masa in-nuur.
Colloquial 'no' ends in a glottal stop, written '. It is not the MSA laa.
The entry is spelled with ت, matching speech (MSA ثوم is said toom). The vowel is long oo.
Form II imperative, with a doubled k. Urban Palestinian says ذ as d, so the vowelled form is respelled with د. The suffix -ni is 'me'.
Form II verb with a doubled s. It is used for explaining and interpreting, though shara7 is the commoner everyday verb for 'explain'.
Palestinian word for a common cold or runny nose, as in 3indi rash7. I am not fully sure of the exact vowelling. zukaam and nazle are also heard.
bi + il- before ت assimilates to bit-tawfii'. The ق in tawfii' is a glottal stop. The hamza of imti7aan is written after the prefix, as bil-'imti7aan.
The article assimilates to the sun letter ص, giving iS-Soomaal, and the vowel is long oo. The country name is used as in MSA.

meaning_fix: Gospel / the New Testament (the whole Bible is il-kitaab il-muqaddas)
reasoning: Injiil means the Gospel or New Testament, not the whole Bible. The word-initial hamza is not written in the romanization.
A religious formula, so ق keeps [q] per the scheme's rule for religious words, though some speakers say ta'abbal. The shadda doubles b.
Construct state of the taa marbuta, so faatuurat, and I respell with ت so it is voiced. Palestinian 'water' is mayy. The construct vowel (-at or -it) is not certain.
shu is the Palestinian 'what'. The hamza of awlaad is written after il- (il-'awlaad), while word-initial akhbaar has no written hamza. Taa marbuta after س is e.
fii is 'there is', and 3addaad is a meter with a doubled d. It applies to taxi, electricity or water meters.
'addeesh is the Palestinian 'how much' with a glottal stop and a doubled d. saakin is the masculine singular participle, so this is addressed to a man. hoon has long oo.
The dual ending is -een in Palestinian, not MSA -ayn. The word-initial hamza is not written.
Taa marbuta after ب is e. maktabe covers both a bookstore and a library.
bi + yiswa contracts to biswa, by analogy with biktub, and means 'is worth'. It is common in ma biswa (not worth it). The vowelling is my best judgment.
The standard phrase for a deceased man. The suffix 'him' is -u (written و), and w- attaches directly to yighfirlu. Allaah has a doubled l.
